info.name: LLM Arena
info.description:
Manual verification for LLM Arena's API. Import this, then work top to bottom.

## First time

1. Import `docs/llm-arena.postman_environment.template.json` alongside this collection and select it in the environment picker. Optional — the collection works standalone on its own variables — but it keeps your Clerk secret out of the collection file, and the filled-in copy is gitignored.
2. Start the app: `pnpm dev`. Check `baseUrl` matches the port it actually claimed — it falls back to 3001 if 3000 is taken.
3. Put your Clerk **secret** key (`sk_test_...`, from `.env.local`) in `clerkSecretKey`. If you skip the environment and use the collection variable instead, fill the **Current value** column, not Initial value — Initial value is what gets exported and committed.
4. Run the four **Setup** requests in order. They find a user, open a session, and save a short-lived JWT into `sessionToken`, which every Chat request then uses.
5. Run **Revoke session** when you're finished. Tokens last 15 minutes; if Chat starts returning 401, mint a new one.

The Setup scripts write to the active environment when there is one and to the collection otherwise, so either setup works — but don't half-do it. An environment that defines `sessionToken` shadows the collection's, so a stale empty value there beats a good value here.

## Reading a chat response

`/api/chat` returns an SSE stream, not JSON. Postman shows the raw event lines. The two worth reading:

- `"type":"start"` — carries the `modelId`, so parallel streams are tellable apart.
- `"type":"finish"` — carries the real measured numbers: `timeToFirstTokenMs`, `tokensPerSecond`, `outputTokens`, `totalMs`.

`tokensPerSecond` is `null` when the provider returned everything in one chunk. That is correct — there is no rate to measure — not a bug.

No cost field anywhere. Every model here is free tier.

## One model per request

There is no endpoint that takes three models. The arena sends three of these in parallel, each with one `modelId`, so a slow or failing model cannot take the other two answers down. To imitate the real thing, open three tabs and send them together.

## Re-importing after a route is added

This collection is regenerated in the repo, not edited in Postman. When it changes, import the file again — the fixed `_postman_id` means Postman recognises it and offers to replace the existing copy instead of creating a duplicate. Choose replace.

That resets collection variable values, which is the other reason to keep your Clerk secret in the environment: environments are separate objects and survive a replace untouched.

Edits made in the Postman UI are lost on the next replace. If you want something kept, put it in the file.

## Not here yet

Threads, turns, votes, and the leaderboard don't exist as endpoints yet (scope.md features 3, 6, and 9). This collection grows as they land.

variable.description: Where the dev server is actually listening.
Clerk sk_test_... from .env.local. Leave empty in git — fill it in your local copy only.
Filled by Setup step 3. Short-lived; re-mint when Chat starts 401ing.
Any free-tier OpenRouter id. See the OpenRouter reference folder for the live list.

item.name: Setup — get a session token
item.description: Clerk's Backend API, not this app. These four exist so a browser sign-in isn't needed to exercise an authenticated endpoint by hand. They authenticate with clerkSecretKey rather than the collection's bearer token.

exec: // Write to the active environment when there is one, otherwise to the
// collection. An environment variable shadows a collection variable of the

// Capture the first user so the next request has someone to open a session for.
console.log('No users in this Clerk instance. Sign up once at ' + pm.variables.get('baseUrl') + '/sign-up first.');

console.log('sessionToken saved to ' + (pm.environment.name || 'the collection') + '. Good for 15 minutes.');

item.name: Turns
item.description:
Creates the turn a prompt belongs to, and the PENDING ModelResponse rows the parallel /api/chat calls fill in.

This endpoint exists to kill a race. One arena prompt is up to three simultaneous POSTs to /api/chat, and if each of those created the turn they share, they would collide. So none of them does — this runs first, alone, in one transaction, and hands back ids nobody else holds.

It calls no model and spends nothing upstream, so it carries no token-bucket cost. Shield and bot detection still apply.

**Run "Create a turn" before anything in the Chat or Votes folders** — everything downstream needs the ids it saves.

exec: // See the Setup folder for why this picks a scope rather than always
console.log('turn ' + turn.turnId + ' created with ' + turn.responses.length + ' pending responses');

request.description:
The happy path, and the starting point for this whole collection. Expect **201** and a body carrying `threadId`, `turnId`, `index`, and one `{ modelResponseId, modelId }` per model.

Omitting `threadId` starts a new conversation. The response rows come back PENDING; nothing has called a model yet.

`name` is the model's display name from the caller's catalog — the server has no catalog of its own (that's feature 5, in the browser). It is stored as a snapshot so a thread still renders properly if a model is later renamed or drops off the free tier, and it is only ever displayed, never used for logic. The `id` beside it is held to the `:free` shape.

Saves `threadId`, `turnId`, `modelResponseId`, `modelResponseIdB` and `pendingModelResponseId` for the requests that follow. The third id is deliberately left unanswered so the Votes folder can prove you cannot vote for a model that hasn't finished.

exec: // See the Setup folder for why this picks a scope rather than always

request.description:
Passing `threadId` adds a turn to a conversation you already own. Expect **201** with `index` one higher than the previous turn.

Turns are numbered per thread, which is what lets a single model's own conversation be replayed in order: the thread's turns by `index`, each prompt paired with that model's response. A model that failed a turn simply contributes nothing to its own history.

Overwrites `turnId` and the response ids, so run "Create a turn" again if you want the original back.

exec: // See the Setup folder for why this picks a scope rather than always

request.description:
A perfectly valid turn with a single model. Expect **201**.

It exists to set up the vote rule: a turn with one answer has nothing to compare, so it can never be voted on. Saves `soloTurnId` and `soloModelResponseId` for the Votes folder.

A well-formed but **paid** OpenRouter id. Expect **400** and the same plain sentence as any other bad body.

This check used to live on /api/chat, because the model id used to travel in that request. It doesn't any more — /api/chat names a response row and reads the model id back off it — so the `:free` requirement moved here, to the one place an id now enters the system. Every model in this arena is free tier, so the suffix is a real requirement, not a formatting preference.

No rows are written and OpenRouter is never called.

Expect **400**. A turn holds one response per model — the database says so with a unique index on (turnId, modelId) — so a repeated id is caught during validation and reported as the plain bad request it is, rather than surfacing as a unique-violation 500.
Expect **400**. The arena compares at most three models at once, so the cap is enforced at the boundary rather than trusted to the picker UI.
Expect **404** and a plain sentence. Nothing is created — a turn is never orphaned onto a thread that isn't there.

Expect **403**, distinct from the 404 above.

Threads are readable by anyone with the link (feature 8), so a thread belonging to someone else is not a secret and doesn't need to be disguised as missing — but writing into one is closed. Reading is open, writing is owned.

**Needs a second Clerk user.** Set `otherUsersThreadId` by hand: run the Setup folder against a different user, create a turn, then switch back. Without that this returns 404, not 403.

Deliberately sends no bearer token. Expect **401** and a plain sentence.

Clerk is checked before Arcjet, so an anonymous caller never reaches a rule. Creating a turn is a write, and writes need a signed-in person.

A scripted-client User-Agent Arcjet recognises. Expect **403** and the shared blocked sentence — no rule name, ever.

This route has shield and bot detection but deliberately **no token bucket**. The bucket on /api/chat is sized in model calls, because that is what costs money; charging a turn against it would quietly change what the number means.

Note bot detection is sticky: after this fires, plain Postman requests from the same client can keep getting 403 for a couple of minutes while the reputation decays. Test bots and rate limits in separate runs.

item.name: Chat
item.description:
Streams one model's answer into a response row that /api/turns already created.

**Run "Create a turn" in the Turns folder first.** The body names a `modelResponseId` and nothing else — no model id, no prompt, no history. Everything that reaches the model is read from the database.

That shape is the result of four rounds of the same bug. The model id used to travel here and could be pointed at another row. Then the prompt could differ from the turn's, so an answer was filed under a question the model never saw. Then the prompt could be right but followed by a trailing assistant turn that steered it. Then the prompt could be right and last, with fabricated history in front of it. Each fix validated one more field; the caller kept finding the next. Nothing is trusted from the browser now because nothing needs to be sent.

The request is `.strict()`, so a stale client still posting `messages` gets a plain 400 rather than having its history silently ignored — which would look like the server obeying it.

In the real arena three of these fire at once, in parallel. Each holds its own response id, so they never race.

request.description:
The happy path. Expect a stream, and watch for the trailing `"type":"finish"` event — that is where timeToFirstTokenMs, tokensPerSecond, outputTokens and totalMs live.

The body carries only the response id. The prompt the model receives is the one the turn recorded, read from the database, so the answer is stored against exactly the text that produced it — by construction, not by a validation the next caller works around.

When the stream closes, those numbers are written to the row along with the answer text and the input/output/total token counts. `costUsd` stays 0.000000: every model here is free tier, so zero is the honest measurement rather than a placeholder. Token totals are stored exactly as the provider reported them and never recomputed from input + output — reasoning and cached-input tokens land in a provider's total differently.

Free models are genuinely slow and sometimes rate-limited upstream. If you get `"type":"error"` with "That model didn't answer", the row is marked FAILED and the real provider error is in the dev server log — that separation is deliberate.

The same prompt, to the turn's second model. In the browser this fires simultaneously with the request above; here, send it right after.

Run it so the turn has two COMPLETE answers — that is what makes the Votes folder work at all. The turn's third model is left alone on purpose, so "Model still answering → 409" has something to prove.

This is also the point of one-request-per-model: if this model is slow or down, the first model's answer is already on screen and untouched.

Run "Continue a thread" in the Turns folder first, then send this with the new `modelResponseId` it saved.

There is no history in this body, and that is the point. The server rebuilds this model's own conversation from the thread: every earlier turn's prompt paired with *this* model's answer to it, in `index` order, then the current turn's prompt last.

Which is what "each model carries its own separate conversation" actually means — three models in one thread can have three different-length transcripts. A model that failed an earlier turn contributes nothing to its own history and simply never saw that exchange.

Deliberately sends no bearer token. Expect 401 and a plain sentence — no stack trace, no Clerk internals. Sending a prompt requires sign-in.

Auth is checked before Arcjet, so an anonymous caller never reaches a rule and never consumes a rate-limit token.

Expect **403** and no model call.

A response id is a cuid, so guessing one isn't the threat. A shared thread link handing its ids to a signed-in stranger is — and that stranger must not be able to spend this app's upstream budget filling in someone else's turn. Reading a thread is open; writing into one is owned.

**Needs a second Clerk user** — set `otherUsersModelResponseId` by hand, the same way as "Someone else's thread" in the Turns folder.

A body in the old shape: invented earlier questions, invented earlier answers, and the turn's genuine prompt last. Expect **400**, and no model is called.

This is the request that closed the loop. Every earlier version of the prompt binding accepted it — the real prompt was present, it was the last message, and nothing checked what came before it. The fabricated exchange would have reached the model and shaped its answer, and that answer plus its speed numbers would have been stored as the response to the canonical turn.

It cannot be validated away, because the whole array is the caller's invention. The fix was to stop accepting it: the server already holds the real transcript, so it builds one. `.strict()` turns the leftover field into an honest 400 rather than a silent ignore.
Expect **404** and a plain sentence. The row is looked up before the provider is called, so a bad id costs nothing upstream.

Send "Send a prompt" first, let it finish, then send this. Expect **409**, "That model has already answered this prompt."

COMPLETE is the one status a row can never leave. Without that a finished row could be re-run indefinitely, each run spending a real upstream call and overwriting a real measurement — and the vote rule depends on the count of completed answers never falling.

Fire this at a PENDING row while another copy of the same request is still streaming — two Postman tabs, or the Runner.

Expect the second one to return **409**, "That model is already answering this prompt."

Claiming a row is a conditional update, not a read-then-check, so exactly one caller can win it. Before that fix both callers read PENDING, both spent an upstream call, and the slower one silently overwrote the faster one's answer and metrics.

A reservation expires after two minutes — comfortably past the route's own 60s `maxDuration` — so a stream that dies mid-flight cannot lock the row forever.

Send this once a response row has ended up FAILED. Free models are rate-limited upstream constantly, so waiting for a real one rarely takes long.

Expect it to be **accepted and stream normally**. FAILED is deliberately not terminal: a transient provider error costing a model its slot in a turn permanently would make the arena's comparison less honest, not more. COMPLETE is the only status that closes a row for good.

Sends a scripted-client User-Agent that Arcjet recognises. Expect 403 and a plain sentence, with no model ever called. The refusal is deliberately identical for bot and shield denials — telling a caller which rule caught them helps an attacker and helps a real user not at all.

Postman and curl are on the allow list on purpose: hand-verification through them is the only test path this project has. Every other automated client is denied. Note the ordering — bot detection runs before the rate limit, so this still returns 403 even when the bucket is already empty.

Not a single-shot request — send it repeatedly to drain the bucket.

The limit is a token bucket keyed by the signed-in Clerk user, not by IP: capacity 30, refilling 15 per 60s, and one model call spends one token. Because one arena prompt is three parallel calls, that is ten three-model prompts back to back and five a minute sustained.

The body is deliberately empty so nothing upstream is spent while draining it: Arcjet decides before the body is parsed, so each send costs a token and returns 400 until the bucket empties. Expect 400s, then 429 with a plain sentence naming the real seconds to wait. Wait a minute and it allows again.

The bucket is eventually consistent, so denials land a beat late rather than exactly on the request that crosses capacity — a fast local burst can overrun before the 429s start. The spend is bounded, just not to the precise boundary.

An empty body. Expect **400** and the same plain sentence every malformed request gets, with no detail about which field was wrong.

The schema is `.strict()`, so this also covers a stale client still sending `messages`: it is rejected outright rather than accepted with the history quietly dropped.

Exercises the real provider-failure path, not validation.

**Setup:** create a turn whose model is a well-formed `:free` id that no longer exists on OpenRouter — `ghost/model-that-never-was:free` works — and save the response id it returns as `unknownModelResponseId`. The id passes the shape check, because that check cannot know which ids are real (the live catalog is feature 5), so the failure happens at call time.

Expect **200**, with the stream carrying `"type":"error"` and "That model didn't answer. You can try it again." Never the provider exception, which goes to the server log alone. The row is marked FAILED — and can be retried, see below.

This request previously still sent the old `modelId` field and no `modelResponseId`, so it only ever hit malformed-body validation and had silently stopped testing the thing it is named after.

item.name: Votes
item.description:
One person's pick of the best answer in a turn. **Run the Turns folder first, then stream at least two answers from the Chat folder** — a vote is impossible until two models have actually finished.

That rule is enforced in two places on purpose. The database holds what it can state declaratively: one vote per person per turn, and a winner that genuinely belongs to the turn being voted on (a composite foreign key). The "two or more answered" count lives in the vote transaction, which is safe because a response only ever moves PENDING → COMPLETE or PENDING → FAILED and never back — so the count can rise between check and write, never fall.

Signing in is required; owning the thread is not. The whole point of a shareable arena link is that other people can weigh in.

exec: // See the Setup folder for why this picks a scope rather than always

request.description:
The happy path. Expect **201** with `voteId`, `turnId` and `modelResponseId`.

Requires two of the turn's models to have finished streaming — run "Send a prompt" and "Send the second model's prompt" in the Chat folder first, or this returns 409.

Send this straight after the request above. Expect **409** — "You've already voted on this prompt."

One vote per person per turn is a unique index in the database, not a check in code. That matters: two votes racing each other could both pass an application check, and only the constraint actually closes the window. Changing your mind is not supported by design — the leaderboard is built from honest first reactions.

Run "Create a one-model turn" first, and optionally stream its single answer. Expect **409** — "You can only vote once at least two models have answered."

This is the rule the whole data model was shaped around: a vote is a comparison, and there is nothing to compare. It holds whether the second model is still pending, failed, or was never selected at all.

Votes for the third model of the opening turn — the one deliberately left unstreamed. Expect **409**, "That model hasn't finished answering yet."

The turn itself is votable (two others finished), so this is specifically about the chosen answer. The composite foreign key would accept this row happily — it only checks the response belongs to the turn — so the status check has to live in the transaction.

A votable turn, and a real response id — from a different turn. Expect **400**, "That answer isn't part of this prompt."

The transaction catches it first and answers plainly. Behind it, the database would refuse the write anyway: `Vote(modelResponseId, turnId)` is a composite foreign key onto `ModelResponse(id, turnId)`, so a mismatched pair cannot physically be stored. Belt and braces, deliberately — this is the one invariant that would silently corrupt the leaderboard if it ever slipped.
Expect **404** and a plain sentence. Nothing is written.
Missing `modelResponseId` and an empty `turnId`. Expect **400** and the same plain sentence every malformed body gets. No detail about which field was wrong reaches the caller.
Expect **401**. Reading a thread is open to everyone; voting is a write and needs a signed-in person, because a vote is attributed to one.

item.name: OpenRouter reference
item.description: OpenRouter directly, not this app. Handy for grabbing a real model id, and it's the same catalog the model picker will use in scope.md feature 5.

exec: // Print the free tier sorted by context window — the same order the picker will use.
console.log(free.length + ' free models. Top 10 by context window:');

request.description: Public, no key needed. Open the Postman console after sending — the script prints the free tier sorted by context window so you can paste an id into the modelId variable.
